locations.name: Kalgoorlie
locations.depot: our Fremantle depot, carted east up the Great Eastern Highway through Southern Cross and Coolgardie
locations.leadTime: Usually 7-12 business days from order to on the ground, and faster when a truck is already running east
locations.truck: Tilt-tray for 10ft and 20ft where the approach is firm; side loader or crane truck for 40ft and for anything lifted into a fenced compound
locations.metaDesc: Shipping containers for sale and hire in Kalgoorlie. Carted east from Fremantle for Goldfields mine sites, workshops, yards and homes. Call 1300 467 776.
locations.line: Six hundred kilometres of Great Eastern Highway separates the Goldfields from the nearest port, and that one fact shapes every container decision made in Kalgoorlie. Cartage is not a rounding error out here. The way to keep it sensible is to travel on a truck already heading east rather than sending one out for a single box, which means being a bit flexible about the day and very precise about the specification. Nobody wants the wrong container standing in a yard at Boulder with six hundred kilometres of highway between it and anywhere it could be swapped.
locations.uses: core trays and sample storage for exploration crews working the ground out toward Menzies, Leonora and Kambalda, consumable and tool stores on drill programs where the nearest hardware counter is hours away, parts and workshop storage across the Anzac Drive and Broadwood industrial blocks, dry lock-up for prospectors keeping detectors, dry blowers and jerry cans out of the red dust, crib rooms and site offices on short-life packages, and household storage while a Boulder miner's cottage gets underpinned and reroofed
access: Kalgoorlie is one of the rare Australian towns where the street layout works in a truck driver's favour. Hannan Street and the grid around it were set out wide enough to turn a camel team, and a rigid with six metres hanging off the back inherits the benefit. Most of the town centre, and the newer estates out at Somerville and Hannans, give a driver room to set up square and take his time. Boulder is tighter. The lanes behind Burt Street, the old cottages on narrow frontages and the rear laneways were never sized for a loaded truck, and the verges are soft red gravel that cuts up badly under a rear axle. Ground is the second question. Much of the Goldfields sits on calcrete and hard red gravel that carries a container beautifully and asks for almost nothing underneath it. What catches people out is transition ground: a pad graded last month and never compacted, fresh fill around a new shed, or the fringe of the salt country out toward Lake Lefroy where a summer storm turns the surface to grease for a day and then bakes it hard again. If the pad is new, say so, and we will bring timber. The third question is heat. Through summer the front half of the day is the working half. Steel that has been standing in the sun since dawn is too hot to put a hand on by eleven, sealant stops behaving, and nobody makes good decisions at forty-four degrees. A morning slot is not fussiness, it is how the job gets done properly. Three photos with your enquiry settle most of it: the street looking in, the length of the approach, and the spot itself. Send those and we will tell you which truck is coming and what day it can be there.

sections.h: Getting a container up the Great Eastern Highway
p: Every container that lands in Kalgoorlie has already done a long day on the road, and that changes how you should order. Two things make the difference between a sensible number and a silly one. The first is timing: a unit that can travel on a truck already scheduled east is a very different proposition to one that needs a truck sent out on its own account. The second is batching. Two or three containers going to the same job, or to the same street, share a run and share the cost of it. If you know you will need a second box in a month, it is worth saying so at the first enquiry.

The other thing that saves money out here is getting the specification right the first time. In Perth or Brisbane, swapping a wrong unit is an inconvenience. In Kalgoorlie it is a second linehaul. So we ask more questions than you might expect: what is going inside it, how long for, does it need a personnel door or extra vents, is it going onto a hardstand or onto dirt, will site want it painted. Ring 1300 467 776 with the address and the job and we will come back with the container and the cartage as one number, so there is nothing waiting on the invoice.

sections.h: Red dust, heat and what they do to a steel box
p: Goldfields dust is fine, it is relentless, and it gets into everything with a moving part. The two places it matters on a container are the door seals and the locking gear. Grit works its way into the rubber and along the cam rods, and a set of doors that opened sweetly in the yard becomes a two-person job after a windy fortnight. A wipe of the seals and a smear of grease on the cams and hinges a couple of times a year is the whole maintenance program, and it is the difference between a container that lasts thirty years and one that annoys you every time you open it. A lockbox is worth having as much for keeping dust out of the padlock as for security.

Heat is the other one. A closed steel box in a Kalgoorlie February gets a long way past the outside temperature, and while that does not hurt tools or steel stock, it is hard on anything with electronics, adhesives, aerosols or batteries in it. Vents help. So does whirlybird ventilation, a light-coloured roof, and leaving a hundred millimetres of air under the floor rather than sitting the box flat on the ground. Dry heat means condensation is less of an issue here than on the coast, but the cold clear nights in July still swing thirty degrees off the afternoon, and that is enough to sweat a poorly ventilated container.

sections.h: Mine sites, exploration camps and site access
p: A good share of Goldfields containers never see a residential street. They go to a mine gate, a camp or a drill pad, and those deliveries live or die on paperwork organised well before the truck leaves. Site access permits, driver inductions, gate hours, escort requirements, wash-down and speed limits on the haul road are all normal and all specific to the site. We need the site contact, the gate the truck is expected at, and what the site expects to do with the container when it arrives, because plenty of operations would rather offload with their own franna or telehandler than have a side loader working inside their fence line.

Out past the gate it is a different set of questions again. Exploration camps and remote pads are usually at the end of a graded track, and a graded track is fine for a light vehicle and marginal for a loaded truck. Corrugations, washouts after a storm, and soft sand through creek crossings are the usual culprits. Where a truck cannot safely reach the final spot, the sensible answer is to drop at the nearest hardstand and let the site shift it the last few kilometres with gear built for it. Tell us the truth about the track at the quote stage and we will plan for it rather than discovering it at three in the afternoon.

faqs.q: How long does a container take to get to Kalgoorlie?
faqs.a: Usually seven to twelve business days from order to on the ground. The container itself is rarely the hold-up. What sets the date is when a truck is next running east with room on the deck, and whether the unit needs anything fitted before it goes, like extra vents, a personnel door or a paint job. If you have a fixed date, a shutdown, a site start or a lease ending, tell us at the enquiry and we will work backwards from it. Ordering a fortnight early costs nothing and buys you the good end of that range.

faqs.q: Can you deliver straight to a mine site or exploration camp out past Leonora?
faqs.a: Yes, and we do it regularly, but the site controls how it happens. We need the site contact, the gate, the induction and permit requirements, and the site's preference on offloading, because many operations would rather use their own franna or telehandler than have our truck working inside the fence. Beyond the gate, the honest question is what the access track is like. Corrugations and soft creek crossings stop a loaded truck that a ute drives through without noticing. If the last leg is marginal we will drop at the nearest hardstand and let the site do the final shift.

faqs.q: Will things be safe stored in a container through a Kalgoorlie summer?
faqs.a: Tools, steel, drill consumables, furniture and general gear are fine. What struggles is anything with electronics, batteries, aerosols or adhesives in it, because a sealed steel box in February runs well above the outside temperature. Vents make a real difference, whirlybirds more so, and getting the floor off the ground on sleepers or pads lets air move underneath. A light roof colour helps too. If you are storing something genuinely heat-sensitive, tell us before you order and we will spec the ventilation properly rather than you retrofitting it in the dust later.

faqs.q: Can I look at the container before it comes east?
faqs.a: Stock for the Goldfields is picked up at our Fremantle depot, and inspection there is by arrangement rather than a walk-in, so ring 1300 467 776 first and we will organise a time and have the unit accessible. If a trip to the coast is not realistic, which for most Kalgoorlie buyers it is not, ask for photos of the actual unit on request and we will send them before delivery: corner castings, door end, roof, and a shot down the floor. You get to see the box you are buying, not a stock image of one like it.

locations.name: Bunbury
locations.depot: our Fremantle depot, a straight run down the Forrest Highway of about two hours
locations.leadTime: Usually 3-6 business days from order to on the ground
locations.truck: Tilt-tray for 10ft and 20ft; crane truck or side loader for 40ft and for the older streets around East and South Bunbury
locations.metaDesc: Shipping containers for sale and hire in Bunbury. Short-haul from Fremantle to the South West, with honest advice on sand, estuary ground and salt air.
locations.line: Bunbury is the easy one on this list. The Forrest Highway puts a truck here in about two hours from the depot, there is a working port in town, and the industrial land at Picton and Davenport is flat, sealed and built for heavy vehicles. So the interesting part of a Bunbury job is never getting the container to Bunbury. It is the last thirty metres, where coastal sand carries far less than it looks like it should, the low ground near the estuary stays soft most of winter, and a peppermint tree has had sixty years to lean out over the road.
locations.uses: lay-down and consumable storage for the mineral sands and alumina contractors working out of Picton, Kemerton and Worsley, parts and trade storage across the Davenport and Glen Iris industrial estates, dairy and machinery storage on the farms through Brunswick Junction, Harvey and Roelands, orchard and packing shed storage around Donnybrook, gear and barrel storage for the Ferguson Valley wineries, boat, dive and crab gear for people on the Australind and Eaton side of the estuary, and site stores on the constant run of builds through Dalyellup and Treendale
access: Three quite different sorts of Bunbury address, and they need three different answers. The industrial belt is the simple one. Picton, Davenport, Glen Iris and out toward Kemerton were laid out for trucks, the aprons are sealed, the gates are wide, and there is usually a forklift or a loader already on site. Those drops get booked and done, often with a 40ft, which is not true of most towns this size. The second is the older residential core. East Bunbury, South Bunbury, College Grove and the streets running back off Ocean Drive were subdivided long before anybody imagined a twelve metre truck, with narrow verges, limestone kerbs, and Norfolk Island pines and peppermints that hang low over the carriageway. Plenty of those blocks are perfectly deliverable, but by crane over the fence rather than by tilt-tray up the side, and that is a decision worth making a week out rather than on the morning. Third is ground, and it is the one people underestimate. The coastal strip from Dalyellup up through the CBD and on to Australind is sand, and dry sand carries almost nothing. A corner casting concentrates a couple of tonne onto a plate the size of a dinner plate, and it will find the soft spot. On the low ground either side of the Leschenault estuary and along the Collie and Preston river flats you get the opposite problem: peaty, high water table country that is firm in February and greasy in July. We would rather bring ply and timber and spread the load than pull a truck out of your front lawn. Rural blocks up the Ferguson Valley add a fourth wrinkle, with steep gravel driveways, single-lane bridges and low marri branches. Photos from the street, along the approach and at the spot itself sort nearly all of it out in advance.

sections.h: A short run down the Forrest Highway
p: Most of regional Western Australia takes what it can get when it comes to containers. Bunbury does not have to. Two hours from the depot means the cartage on a South West job is a sensible number rather than the largest line on the quote, and it means you get an actual choice: 10ft, 20ft, 40ft, standard height or high cube, single door or double, and a real conversation about grade rather than being handed whichever unit happens to be standing closest to the gate. If you want a specific configuration, asking for it here is not wishful thinking. The grades page sets out what each condition means and what is checked before a unit leaves.

Short-haul also means flexibility when something goes wrong, and something occasionally does. A driveway that has gone soft after a wet week, a slab that is not poured yet, a site that is not ready on the day. Pulling a booking and re-running it is a couple of hours of truck time from here, not a wasted day of linehaul, so we can be reasonable about it. The same applies if you decide a 20ft was optimistic and you want a 10ft instead. Ring 1300 467 776 with the address and what the container is for and we will quote the box and the cartage together as one figure.

sections.h: Sand, estuary ground and what goes under the corners
p: A shipping container carries its whole weight through four corner castings, so the only ground that matters is the four spots those castings land on. On the Bunbury coastal strip that ground is sand, usually with a thin skin of turf over it, and it will let a loaded corner settle a hundred millimetres in the first wet winter without any warning at all. What you notice is not the sinking. What you notice is that the doors stop lining up, because once the four corners are no longer at the same height the whole frame starts working against itself and a racked container is a container you fight with every time you open it.

Concrete pads or hardwood sleepers under the four corners, bedded in and checked level across both diagonals, prevent all of it and cost very little. On the low estuary ground at Australind, Eaton and along the river flats, add height: get the floor a hundred millimetres or more clear of the ground so air moves under it and the underside is not sitting against damp soil for the next twenty years. That also means the container can be lifted cleanly if you ever sell up or reconfigure the yard, rather than having to be dug out. Tell us at the quote if the ground is sandy, sloping or soft and we will put the timber on the truck.

sections.h: Salt air on the South West coast
p: Anything steel within a kilometre or two of the water at Bunbury lives a harder life than the same thing at Donnybrook, and a container is no exception. The good news is that a shipping container is built from corten steel to sit on the deck of a ship in the open ocean for twenty-five years, so it starts from a far better place than a colorbond shed does. The bad news is that the places salt does its work are the places people forget: the underside where spray settles and never dries, the door hinges and cam gear, and any spot where the paint has been scraped through to bare metal during handling.

The maintenance that actually matters is not complicated. Get it up off the ground so the underside dries out. Touch up scrapes with a cold galvanising or a decent enamel before they go orange rather than after. Grease the hinges and locking bars once or twice a year. Keep the roof clear of leaf litter so water runs off instead of ponding in a corner, which is the single most common cause of a rust patch on the top of an otherwise sound box. Do that on a coastal Bunbury block and the container will outlast most of what you build around it.

faqs.q: How quickly can you deliver a container to Bunbury?
faqs.a: Three to six business days is the normal window, and it can be quicker on a standard 20ft going to an address with clear access. Bunbury benefits from being a short run down the Forrest Highway from the depot rather than a linehaul, so we are not waiting for a truck heading that way once a fortnight. What stretches it is a crane booking, a unit that needs modification first, or wet weather on soft ground where waiting two days beats bogging a truck in your paddock. Give us your date at the enquiry and we will build the run around it.

faqs.q: Can you deliver further south, to Busselton, Margaret River or Manjimup?
faqs.a: Yes. Anything from Harvey down through Busselton, Dunsborough, Margaret River, Nannup, Bridgetown and Manjimup runs on the same road out of the depot, so it is an extension of a Bunbury job rather than a separate exercise. Timing is similar, sometimes a day longer. What changes is access: the karri and jarrah country has narrow gravel driveways, steep pinches and low branches, and a 40ft that is straightforward on a Picton hardstand is a genuine conversation on a Nannup bush block. Send photos of the approach and we will tell you what will fit before you settle on a size.

faqs.q: Will a container rust quickly this close to the ocean?
faqs.a: Not if it is set up properly. Containers are built from corten steel to cross oceans on an open deck, so salt air is nothing new to them. The three things that shorten their life on a coastal block are all avoidable: sitting flat on damp ground so the underside never dries, leaf litter ponding water on the roof, and handling scrapes left bare until they go orange. Get it up on pads, keep the roof clear, touch up bare metal, and grease the hinges and locking gear once or twice a year. That is the whole program.

faqs.q: What size fits on a typical Bunbury block?
faqs.a: A 20ft is the sensible ceiling on most suburban blocks around Bunbury and Australind. It is six metres long and needs roughly nine or ten metres of straight run to place, which most side yards and driveway aprons can find. A 40ft usually means giving up side access altogether and it needs close to twenty metres of clear approach, so it belongs on acreage or a commercial yard. If you need volume rather than footprint, a 20ft high cube gives you an extra 300mm of internal height on the same ground area, and it is worth asking about.

locations.name: Geraldton
locations.depot: our Fremantle depot, roughly four and a half hours north on the Brand Highway
locations.leadTime: Usually 5-9 business days from order to on the ground
locations.truck: Tilt-tray for 10ft and 20ft; side loader or crane truck for 40ft, with lifts booked for the morning where possible
locations.metaDesc: Shipping containers for sale and hire in Geraldton. Carted up the Brand Highway for fishing, grain, mining and Mid West farm jobs. Call 1300 467 776.
locations.line: Wind decides more Geraldton deliveries than anything else does. The southerly comes in hard most summer afternoons and it has no respect at all for a container hanging off a crane hook, because an empty 20ft is a very effective sail. So lifts get booked early in the day and occasionally get moved when the forecast is ugly. Everything else about Geraldton is straightforward by the standards of remote Western Australia: a sealed run up the Brand Highway, a town that has moved freight through its port for a century, and industrial ground at Narngulu that a truck can actually use.
locations.uses: pot, rope and gear storage for the rock lobster boats working out of the Fishing Boat Harbour and up the coast at Port Denison and Kalbarri, grain, fertiliser and machinery storage on the farms through Chapman Valley, Mullewa, Mingenew and Northampton, lay-down stores for the mineral sands and iron ore contractors around Narngulu and Oakajee, gear storage for the wind farm and solar crews working the Mid West, secure site stores on the estates going in at Wandina and Glenfield, and dry lock-up for boats, dive gear and camping kit that will not fit in a Tarcoola Beach garage
access: The first thing a driver checks for a Geraldton job is the forecast, not the map. From October through March the sea breeze routinely gets into the high twenties and low thirties of knots by early afternoon, and there is a real difference between a tilt-tray drop, which will still go ahead, and a crane lift, which will not. An empty container swinging on a hook in that much wind is dangerous to everybody standing near it, so crane jobs are booked for the morning and we would rather move a lift a day than push it. The second thing is ground, and Geraldton has an unusual version of it. Most of the town sits on sand over coastal limestone, which is a strange combination: the limestone underneath is as good a bearing surface as you could ask for, and the sand on top of it is not. On a block where the caprock is shallow you can put a container down on four pads and never think about it again. On the deep dune sand out at Tarcoola Beach, Drummond Cove or Sunset Beach it will settle unevenly through the first winter unless it is set up properly. The third is the shape of the town. Narngulu and the Webberton and Wonthella light industrial areas are easy, with room and hardstand. The older streets down through Beachlands, Bluff Point and the West End are tighter, with narrow verges, limestone walls right on the boundary and services strung across the frontage. Out on the Moresby Range side the driveways climb hard off the road and a tilt-tray bed will ground before the container clears it. Photos from the street, up the approach and at the spot, plus a note about which way the block faces, and we can call the truck and the time of day in one go.

sections.h: Working around the Geraldton wind
p: People who live here stop noticing the wind. Crane operators do not. The practical effect on a container delivery is simple: a lift over a fence or a house needs the load under control the whole way, and a six metre steel box with nothing in it behaves like a sail once the breeze is over about twenty-five knots. Rather than pretend otherwise, we book Geraldton crane work for the early part of the day, keep an eye on the forecast in the forty-eight hours beforehand, and ring you the afternoon before if it looks like it is going to be a bad one. Moving a lift by a day costs nobody anything. Dropping a container into a fence costs everybody a great deal.

It also feeds into what you should ask for. Where a site can be reached by tilt-tray, a tilt-tray is more weather-tolerant and generally the better answer in a windy town. That sometimes means clearing a bit of yard, taking a gate off its hinges for an hour or moving a car, and it is usually worth the trouble. Where a crane is genuinely the only way in, tell us early so we can get it into a morning slot rather than squeezing it onto the end of a day.

sections.h: Sand over limestone, and getting it level
p: The Batavia Coast has a bearing surface most of Australia would envy sitting somewhere under it. Coastal limestone carries anything you put on it. The problem is knowing how far down it is on your particular block, because the sand above it varies from a few hundred millimetres in the older parts of town to metres of loose dune out at Sunset Beach and Drummond Cove. If you have dug post holes on the block, you already know the answer and it is worth telling us. If you have not, assume sand and set the container up accordingly, because it costs almost nothing to do it right and it is a substantial job to fix afterwards.

The setup that works everywhere here is four concrete pads or hardwood sleepers under the corner castings, bedded down to firm material and checked level across both diagonals, with the floor sitting a hundred millimetres or more clear of the ground. That keeps the doors square, keeps air moving under the floor, and keeps windblown sand from building up against the underside, which is where corrosion starts on a coastal block. If the ground falls away at all, put the doors on the high side. A container that settles even slightly toward its door end turns an easy one-handed job into a shoulder-into-it job.

sections.h: Farm deliveries through the Mid West
p: A good share of Geraldton area containers never stop in town. They go out to properties through Chapman Valley, Northampton, Mullewa, Mingenew and Yuna, and farm deliveries have their own rhythm. The obvious one is harvest. From roughly late September through December nobody on a wheat property has an hour to stand around watching a truck, and depending on conditions there can be vehicle movement restrictions on the district. Getting a container in before the header starts or after the last load has gone to the bin is easier on everybody, and if it has to happen mid-harvest we need a farm contact who can actually answer a phone on the day.

The other one is the last few kilometres. A gravel farm road that carries a road train in dry weather is a different animal after twenty millimetres of rain, and the pinch points are always the same: the grid, the creek crossing, the gateway that was set out for a tractor. Tell us what the access is honestly, including how tight the house gate is and whether there is a tree over the track, and we will bring the right truck. Where the final position is not reachable, dropping on the hardstand near the sheds and letting the loader shift it is often the sensible answer.

faqs.q: How long does delivery to Geraldton take?
faqs.a: Usually five to nine business days from order to on the ground. The run up the Brand Highway is sealed the whole way and reasonably quick, so the timing is mostly about when a truck is heading north with room on it and whether the unit needs anything fitted first. Crane jobs can add a day or two because they have to fit a morning slot with a workable forecast. If you have a fixed date, tell us at the enquiry rather than after, and order a week earlier than you think you need to.

faqs.q: Can wind actually delay my delivery?
faqs.a: A crane lift, yes. A tilt-tray drop, almost never. Once the Geraldton southerly gets past about twenty-five knots an empty container on a hook becomes a sail and the lift is no longer safe for anyone standing near it, so we book crane work in the morning and watch the forecast in the two days beforehand. If it looks bad we will ring you the afternoon before and move it rather than turn up and stand around. If your site can be reached by tilt-tray instead, that is the more weather-proof option and worth a bit of yard clearing.

faqs.q: Can you deliver out to a farm at Mullewa, Northampton or Yuna?
faqs.a: Yes, and it is a big part of what we do in the Mid West. Two things we need to know. First, timing around harvest, because from late September into December a property has no spare hands and there can be movement restrictions on the district. Second, the honest state of the farm road: the grid, the creek crossing, the house gate and any tree over the track. If the final position cannot be reached safely with a loaded truck, we drop on hardstand near the sheds and your loader does the last shift, which is usually a five minute job.

faqs.q: Can I see the container before it is sent to Geraldton?
faqs.a: Stock heading north is picked up from our Fremantle depot and inspection there is by arrangement, so ring 1300 467 776 first and we will set a time and have the unit accessible. For most Geraldton buyers the drive is not worth it, so ask for photos of the actual unit on request and we will send them before delivery: the corners, the door end, the roof and a shot down the length of the floor. If something in the photos is not what you expected, we sort it out before it goes on a truck, not after.

locations.name: Port Hedland
locations.depot: our Fremantle depot, with roughly sixteen hundred kilometres of Great Northern and North West Coastal Highway between there and the Pilbara
locations.leadTime: Usually 2-4 weeks from order to on the ground, and longer through the wet season
locations.truck: Side loader or crane truck for most Pilbara work, since 40ft is common and site cranes are not always free; tilt-tray for 10ft and 20ft into town addresses
locations.metaDesc: Shipping containers for sale and hire in Port Hedland and South Hedland. Honest lead times, cyclone tie-down and ground prep advice for the Pilbara.
locations.line: Think in weeks, not days. Port Hedland is around sixteen hundred kilometres north of the nearest depot, and the honest answer to how fast a container can get here is that it depends on when a truck next runs this way with room on the deck. From November through April it depends on the weather as well, because the Turner, Yule and De Grey crossings cut the highway after a serious rain event and the port clears out ahead of a cyclone. None of that is a reason not to order. It is the reason to order early and to be specific.
locations.uses: lay-down and consumable stores for the contractors working the port, rail and the Boodarie industrial land, spares and tooling storage for shutdown crews who need everything on site before day one, secure trade stores across the Wedgefield industrial estate, crib rooms, first aid rooms and site offices on construction packages, dry storage on the stations running out toward Marble Bar and Nullagine, and household storage for people arriving on a transfer into South Hedland before a house is ready
access: Hedland splits into two towns for delivery purposes and they behave differently. The West End and the older port-side streets are hemmed in by the harbour, the rail and the stockpiles, with heavy vehicle routes, restricted areas and traffic management that a container truck has to work around rather than through. South Hedland is easier: it was planned in one go, the streets are wide, the estates have room, and a rigid can generally get square to a block without drama. Wedgefield is the best of the lot, purpose-built for industry with hardstand, wide aprons and gear already on site to help. Ground in the Pilbara is mostly excellent. Red laterite gravel and compacted pindan carry a container without complaint, and where a pad has been properly built you can put four castings down and forget about it. The exceptions are worth knowing. The tidal flats around the harbour and out toward Boodarie are soft, saline and unforgiving of a loaded truck, and anything on made-up ground within a year of being placed will still be moving. The wet season changes all of it: what was a hardstand in August is a bog in February, and the black soil pockets around the creek systems hold water long after the rain has stopped. The bigger constraint, though, is the highway itself. When the Turner or the De Grey come up, the road shuts, and it stays shut until the water goes down and the road authority reopens it. Trucks sit and wait, sometimes for days. We build that into the estimate rather than pretending it does not happen. Send site photos, the site contact and the induction requirements with your enquiry, and we will tell you what is realistic on timing before anything gets booked.

sections.h: Wet season, cyclone season and what they do to a date
p: The Pilbara wet runs roughly November to April and it does not affect deliveries gently. A single system parked over the catchments will put the Turner, Yule and De Grey crossings under and close the highway, and a truck already on the road simply stops where it is until the water drops and the road is reopened. When a cyclone is genuinely coming, port operations clear out, sites go into their own cyclone procedures, and nobody is craning anything. A container that would have been on the ground on Thursday can end up being on the ground the following week, and there is no supplier in the country who can promise otherwise, whatever they tell you on the phone.

The way to manage it is not optimism, it is lead time. Order before the wet if you can. If you are planning a shutdown, a camp or a build that needs storage on site in February, place the order in October and let it sit in Hedland waiting for you rather than sitting at Karratha waiting for a road to open. If you need multiple units, order them together so they travel together. Ring 1300 467 776 with the job, the site and the date you actually need it by, and we will be straight with you about whether that date is realistic.

sections.h: Tie-downs, footings and ground preparation
p: Port Hedland sits in the most cyclone-exposed built-up area in Australia, and the wind loads written into the building rules here are nothing like the rest of the country. A shipping container is heavy and low, which helps, but an empty one is a large box with a lot of side area and it is not the immovable object people assume. Where a container is staying put on a site through a season, it should be restrained: chained or bolted to cast-in anchors, screw piles or a footing designed for it, with the restraint detail specified by an engineer who works to the local wind region rather than by a rule of thumb off the internet. We are container people, not structural engineers, and on anything permanent or on a workplace we will tell you to get that detail drawn up properly.

Ground preparation is the other half. A level, compacted pad with the corner points on concrete or heavy timber does three things at once: it keeps the doors square, it keeps the underside out of the wet, and it gives the tie-down something to work against. Get the pad done before the truck arrives, not after, because shifting a container thirty metres once the truck has left is a second delivery. To be plain about what a container is and is not: it keeps rain off from above, and it does nothing to keep floodwater out. Water that reaches the door sill gets past the seals, and an empty box will float and travel if it gets deep enough. Site it high, restrain it properly, and do not treat it as protection from water.

sections.h: Site access, inductions and offloading
p: Very little in Hedland gets delivered to a place with no gate on it. Port, rail, mine and major construction sites all run their own access systems, and the delivery works or fails on that paperwork being done before the truck leaves the last town. What we need from you is the site contact and their phone number, the gate the truck should present at, gate hours, induction and permit requirements, PPE expectations, any escort or wash-down requirement, and whether the site wants to offload with its own crane or telehandler. Sites frequently prefer to do it themselves, which is fine and often faster, but it changes which truck we send.

For town addresses in South Hedland and Wedgefield the questions are more ordinary: overhead services, gate width, what is on the other side of the fence, and whether there is anywhere for a truck to stand without blocking a heavy vehicle route. The single most useful thing you can send is photographs. One from the street looking in, one along the length of the approach, one of the exact spot, and if there is a gate, one of the gate with something in shot for scale. Those four pictures answer more questions than a page of description and they get the job planned right the first time, which out here is worth a great deal more than it is in a capital city.

faqs.q: How long does a container take to reach Port Hedland?
faqs.a: Plan on two to four weeks from order to on the ground in the dry, and allow more between November and April. The distance is only part of it. The date is really set by when a truck runs north with room on the deck, and a container that travels on a scheduled run rather than a dedicated trip is a very different proposition. Wet season adds road closures at the river crossings that nobody can plan around. If you have a shutdown or a site start date, order well ahead of it and tell us the date at the enquiry.

faqs.q: Can you still deliver during the wet or cyclone season?
faqs.a: Yes, but with honest caveats. Trucks run all year. What stops them is the highway going under at the Turner, Yule or De Grey crossings, which happens most wets and can hold a load up for days, and a cyclone warning, which shuts down port operations and site craning entirely. We will not give you a hard date in February that we cannot stand behind. What we will do is tell you where your container is, what the road is doing, and what the realistic window looks like. Ordering before the wet is always the better plan.

faqs.q: Does a container need to be tied down in Port Hedland?
faqs.a: If it is staying on a site through cyclone season, it should be restrained, and on a workplace that is not optional. A container is heavy and low, which helps, but an empty one has a lot of side area and is not immovable. The usual approach is chaining or bolting to cast-in anchors, screw piles or a designed footing, on a level compacted pad. The important part is that the restraint detail comes from an engineer working to the local wind region. We can tell you what other Pilbara sites do, but we do not certify tie-downs and would not pretend to.

faqs.q: Can you deliver to a mine site or a station beyond Hedland?
faqs.a: Regularly. For a mine site we need the site contact, the gate, gate hours, induction and permit requirements, and whether the site prefers to offload with its own gear, which many do. For a station run out toward Marble Bar or Nullagine, the question is the track: floodways, sand, and how far it is from the last sealed road. In the wet those tracks are frequently closed and there is nothing to be done about it but wait. Give us the honest description at the quote stage and we will plan the right truck and a realistic date.

locations.name: Karratha
locations.depot: our Fremantle depot, about fifteen hundred kilometres south, often on the same northbound run as Hedland freight
locations.leadTime: Usually 2-4 weeks from order to on the ground; allow longer between December and March
locations.truck: Side loader or crane truck for 40ft and for anything going inside a fence line; tilt-tray for 10ft and 20ft into town and Gap Ridge
locations.metaDesc: Shipping containers for sale and hire in Karratha and Dampier. Straight talk on Pilbara lead times, pad prep and cyclone tie-down. Call 1300 467 776.
locations.line: Nothing in Karratha is made in Karratha. The town runs on iron ore, salt and gas, and virtually every piece of steel in it arrived on the back of a truck that came fifteen hundred kilometres up the North West Coastal Highway. Containers are no different. What that buys you is a freight network well practised at moving big awkward things a long way. What it costs you is time and a bit of flexibility, because the trip only makes financial sense on a truck already heading north with room on the deck, and that is not every day of the week.
locations.uses: spares and tooling stores staged ahead of a shutdown or turnaround on the Burrup, lay-down storage across the Gap Ridge and Karratha industrial estates, crib rooms, store rooms and site offices on construction packages, contractor gear storage for the port and salt operations at Dampier, boat, pot and camping gear for people at Bulgarra, Nickol and Baynton who have run out of garage, station and community storage out through Roebourne, Wickham and Point Samson, and household storage on a Pilbara posting in or out
access: By Pilbara standards Karratha is a comfortable town to deliver into. It was planned rather than grown, the roads are wide, the roundabouts are truck-sized, and the industrial estates at Gap Ridge and out along the Dampier Road were built for exactly this sort of work. Hardstand is common, most commercial sites have a telehandler or a franna available, and 40ft units are ordinary here in a way they are not in a town of this size on the east coast. Residential Karratha is straightforward too, with most of Bulgarra, Nickol, Pegs Creek and Baynton offering a driveway a rigid can get square to. The complications are elsewhere. The Burrup and the Dampier road corridor mean site access controls, gate passes and heritage-restricted areas, and none of that is negotiable on the day, so it has to be sorted before a truck leaves. Ground is generally very good: compacted red laterite gravel is one of the better surfaces in the country for standing a container on. The exceptions are the tidal flats between town and Dampier, which are soft and salty and will swallow a rear axle, and any pad built inside the last few months that has not had a wet season to settle. Rock is the other side of that coin, because on the ridge blocks you can hit stone a few hundred millimetres down, which is excellent bearing but makes it hard to get four points at the same level without a bit of work. Then there is the wet. From December to March the ground softens, the creeks come up, and cyclone warnings stop craning altogether. Send photos of the site, the approach and the gate, plus the site contact and induction requirements, and we will tell you what is realistic before anything gets booked.

sections.h: Everything here arrives on a truck
p: The single biggest lever on what a Karratha container costs you is not the container. It is whether it travels on a truck that was going north anyway. A unit that can wait a week or two for a scheduled run is a completely different exercise to one that has to leave on Tuesday because somebody forgot to order it. That is worth saying plainly, because it is the one thing a customer can control and most people do not realise they can. Give us a window rather than a date, and give us as much notice as the job allows, and we will get your unit onto the right run.

The second lever is batching. Two, three or six containers going to the same site travel far better together than they do one at a time across three months, and if you know a project will need more than one, order them as a group even if the second one sits in a lay-down yard for a few weeks. The third is specification. Getting the size, door configuration, ventilation, personnel door and paint right before the container leaves the depot avoids the one genuinely expensive mistake available to you out here, which is sending a container back down the highway. Ring 1300 467 776 with the job and the site and we will quote the unit and the cartage as one figure.

sections.h: Pads, footings and cyclone restraint on the Burrup coast
p: Karratha is in a severe wind region and the way a container is set up here reflects that. Two separate things matter. The first is the pad. A level, compacted gravel pad with concrete pads or heavy hardwood under the four corner castings keeps the frame square, keeps the underside out of the wet, and gives a set of doors that still line up in three years. Get it built before the delivery, because moving a container after the truck has gone is a second delivery, not an adjustment. Where the block has rock close to the surface, plan on a bit of work to get four points at the same height rather than shimming it later with whatever is lying around.

The second is restraint. A container is heavy, but an empty one presents a great deal of side area to a cyclonic wind and it is not immovable. Where the unit is staying through the season, and certainly on any workplace, it should be tied down to cast-in anchors, screw piles or a designed footing, and the detail for that should come from an engineer working to the local wind region. We are not engineers and will not sign off on a tie-down. What we will do is deliver it onto a pad you have prepared and place it where the restraint can be fitted. One thing to be plain about: a container keeps rain off from above and does nothing against floodwater. Water at door sill height gets past the seals and an empty box will float. Site it high and treat it as storage, not shelter from water.

sections.h: Ordering around a shutdown, and hire versus buying
p: Pilbara work runs on planned dates, and containers should be ordered against those dates rather than against a feeling. If a turnaround starts in six weeks and the spares need to be locked up on site a fortnight before it, the order wants to be placed now, not in a month. That is the difference between a container arriving on a scheduled northbound run and a scramble that costs a great deal more. The same is true in reverse at the end of a project, because the truck that takes a container away has to be going somewhere as well.

Whether to hire or buy usually decides itself on the length of the job. Hire suits a defined program with an end date on it, where you would rather not own an asset in the Pilbara once the crew has gone home and you are not the one arranging the removal. Buying makes more sense the moment the timeframe goes vague or the container is going onto a site that will still be running in five years, because the cartage north is a cost you only want to pay once. That is genuinely the deciding factor out here: freight is the expensive part, so a container that has already made the trip is worth more standing in Karratha than an identical one standing in Fremantle. Tell us the length of the job and we will tell you which way it falls.

faqs.q: How long does delivery to Karratha take?
faqs.a: Two to four weeks from order to on the ground is the usual window in the dry, and December through March can push it out. The date depends less on the distance than on when a truck runs north with room on it, so a customer who can give us a window rather than a fixed day almost always gets a better outcome. Cyclone warnings and wet ground stop craning entirely for a few days at a time. If you are working to a shutdown date, order well ahead of it and say so at the enquiry.

faqs.q: Can you deliver to Dampier, Wickham, Roebourne or Point Samson?
faqs.a: Yes. Those runs work off the same northbound freight as Karratha and are usually the same timing, with the last leg added on. What changes is access. Dampier and the Burrup mean gate passes, site inductions and heritage-restricted areas that have to be organised before the truck leaves, not on arrival. Roebourne and Wickham are straightforward town deliveries. Onslow is further off the highway and worth a separate conversation. Give us the site contact and the induction requirements with the enquiry and we will handle the rest.

faqs.q: Do I need a pad built before the container arrives?
faqs.a: You need four firm, level points, and on most Karratha ground that is easy because compacted red laterite carries a container very well. Concrete pads or heavy hardwood under the corner castings, level across both diagonals, is the standard. Build it before the delivery. Shifting a container after the truck has left is a second delivery, and doing it on the day with whatever timber is on site is how a set of doors ends up out of square. If the block is rocky, allow a bit of time to get four points at the same height.

faqs.q: Should I hire or buy for a Pilbara project?
faqs.a: Length of job decides it. Hire suits a defined program with a finish date, where you would rather not own a container in the Pilbara once the crew has gone and you are not arranging the truck out. Buying gets better as soon as the timeframe goes vague or the site is long-term, because the freight north is the expensive part and you only want to pay it once. That also means a container already standing in Karratha is worth more than the same unit in Fremantle. Tell us the program and we will give you a straight answer.

locations.name: Broome
locations.depot: our Fremantle depot up the coast, or our Darwin depot west along the Victoria and Great Northern Highways, whichever has a truck running
locations.leadTime: Usually 3-5 weeks from order to on the ground in the dry, and the wet season can push it out further
locations.truck: Side loader or crane truck for 40ft and for the industrial addresses; tilt-tray for 10ft and 20ft into town blocks with a firm approach
locations.metaDesc: Shipping containers for sale and hire in Broome and the Kimberley. Honest wet season lead times, pindan ground advice and real delivery planning.
locations.line: Ask about Broome in July and ask about Broome in January and you will get two different answers. Through the dry, a container run up from the south is long but predictable. Through the wet, the Great Northern Highway goes under at Willare and at the Fitzroy crossing, sometimes for days at a stretch, and a truck that left on Monday can still be waiting on Friday for the water to drop. We would rather say that at the enquiry than promise a date we have no business promising and then explain it away later.
locations.uses: gear and equipment storage for the pearling operations working Roebuck Bay and up the coast toward Cygnet Bay, dry lock-up for tour operators putting boats, trailers, swags and camping kit away over the wet, staging and store rooms for freight heading out by barge from the port at Entrance Point, station stores out along the Great Northern Highway toward Derby and Fitzroy Crossing, site stores on the builds going in around Roebuck Estate and Djugun, secure storage for art centres and community organisations, and household storage for people who leave town for the season
access: Broome divides neatly into ground that is easy and ground that is not, and the wet season moves the line between them. The light industrial area off Broome Road, around Clementson and Blackman Streets, is the straightforward end: hardstand, room to work, gear on site, and no drama with a 40ft. New Broome and the Roebuck Estate side have modern streets a rigid can use. Old Broome and Chinatown are the tight end, with narrow lots, boabs and mango trees over the road, verandahs close to the boundary and services strung across frontages, so a crane lift over the fence is frequently the answer rather than a tilt-tray up the side. Cable Beach and the streets behind the dunes are sand, and sand carries almost nothing, so a loaded truck will sit down on a nature strip that looked perfectly firm. Everywhere else it is pindan, that fine red Kimberley soil that compacts hard in the dry and behaves completely differently once the rain starts. In October a pindan track is as good as a road. In February the same track is greasy on top and soft underneath, and the wheel ruts stay in it for a year. Tides matter too, in a way they do not in most towns. Roebuck Bay runs one of the biggest tidal ranges in the country, and anything moving through the port at Entrance Point, particularly barge freight heading to the Dampier Peninsula and the coastal communities, works to a tide window rather than a clock. If your container is going onward by barge, that window drives the date more than the truck does. Send photos of the street, the approach and the exact spot, tell us whether the last leg is sealed or pindan, and we will tell you honestly what can be done and when.

sections.h: The wet season is the schedule
p: From roughly November to April, the Kimberley decides when things arrive. It is not usually the rain falling on Broome that stops a delivery, it is water a long way inland filling the rivers. The Fitzroy crossing and the Willare floodway are the pinch points on the Great Northern Highway, and when they go under the road is closed until it is safe and the road authority reopens it. Trucks stop where they are. Nothing about that is negotiable and no amount of ringing anybody changes it. Cyclones add a second layer, because when one is genuinely coming, everything stops moving and stays stopped until it has passed and the roads have been checked.

So the plan for the Kimberley is always the same: order in the dry. If you need a container on site in February, buy it in September and let it stand in Broome waiting for you. If you need three over the course of a year, order them together and let them travel on one run. If your job is genuinely wet season work, we will still take it on, but the date will be a range and we will keep you posted about where the truck actually is rather than reciting an estimate we stopped believing a week ago. Ring 1300 467 776 with the job and the timing and we will be straight about what is achievable.

sections.h: Pindan, termites and what a steel box is good at
p: There is a reason so much Kimberley storage ends up in containers rather than sheds. A steel box on a decent pad is not interesting to termites, which in this part of the country is a genuine advantage rather than a marketing line, and it does not care much about the build-up humidity that turns a timber structure mouldy. It stands up to the wind better than a light frame shed and it can be picked up and moved to another site when the job changes, which happens a lot up here.

Setting it up on pindan is worth doing properly. Four concrete pads or hardwood sleepers under the corner castings, on ground that has been levelled and compacted, and the floor sitting a hundred millimetres or more clear so air moves underneath and the underside dries out after the wet. Do not sit it flat on the dirt. Ventilation is the other one: through the build-up, humid air gets in and condenses on the underside of a cool roof overnight, and what you notice weeks later is mould on whatever was stored against the ceiling. Vents, whirlybirds and keeping gear up on pallets off the floor deal with almost all of it. And to be plain, a container keeps rain off from above and does nothing against floodwater. Water reaching the door sill gets past the seals, and an empty box will float. Site it on the high part of the block.

sections.h: Going beyond Broome
p: Plenty of the containers we send to the Kimberley do not stop at Broome. They keep going to Derby, out along the highway to Fitzroy Crossing, down to Bidyadanga, up the Cape Leveque road, or onto a barge at Entrance Point bound for a coastal community. Every one of those legs has its own constraints and we would rather map them out at the quote stage than discover them on the day. For a road leg the questions are the surface, the floodways, the width of any gate and whether there is anything on site to help offload. For a barge leg it is the sailing schedule and the tide, and those two decide the date.

Community and station deliveries usually need access arranged in advance, and that is normally organised through the community or the land council rather than by us. It is not a hurdle, it is just something that takes a bit of lead time and cannot be done on the morning of the delivery. The other thing worth planning is what happens when the truck arrives. A remote site with no loader means we need to bring the capability with us, which changes the truck and the timing. Tell us at the start what is available at the far end and everything downstream of that gets easier.

faqs.q: How long does a container take to get to Broome?
faqs.a: Three to five weeks from order to on the ground is a realistic window in the dry, and the wet can push it out further. Distance is only part of the story. The date is set by when a truck runs the Kimberley with room on the deck, whether that is up the coast or across from the Territory. From November to April, road closures at Willare and the Fitzroy crossing are the real variable and they are outside anybody's control. If you know you will need a container next wet season, buy it during the dry and let it wait for you here.

faqs.q: Can you deliver during the wet season?
faqs.a: Trucks run all year, but we will not give you a hard date between November and April that we cannot stand behind. What stops a load is water inland filling the rivers and closing the highway at the Fitzroy crossing or Willare, and a cyclone warning, which stops everything until it has passed and the roads have been checked. What we will do is give you a realistic range, tell you where your container actually is, and let you know as things change. Ordering in the dry for wet season use is always the better plan.

faqs.q: Can you get a container out to a station or a community past Broome?
faqs.a: Yes, to Derby, Fitzroy Crossing, Bidyadanga, up the Cape Leveque road, and by barge from the port to the coastal communities. Each leg has its own constraints. For a road leg we need to know the surface, the floodways, the gate width and what is on site to help offload. For a barge leg the sailing schedule and the tide set the date rather than the truck. Access to community land generally has to be arranged in advance through the community or land council, which is straightforward but takes lead time, so raise it early.

faqs.q: Will things go mouldy in a container through the Broome build-up?
faqs.a: They can, if the container is sealed up tight and the gear is sitting on the floor. Humid air gets in, the roof cools overnight, and moisture condenses on the underside of it and drips. The fix is airflow and elevation: vents or whirlybirds so the air changes over, the container up on pads so the underside dries rather than sitting on damp pindan, and everything stored on pallets rather than directly on the floor. Do that and a container is one of the better places to keep gear in the Kimberley, which is why so many people up here use them instead of a shed.

locations.name: Alice Springs
locations.depot: our Darwin depot, roughly fifteen hundred kilometres straight down the Stuart Highway, or an eastern states unit carted through Adelaide and up the same road from the south
locations.leadTime: Usually 2-4 weeks from order to on the ground
locations.truck: Side loader or crane truck for 40ft and for anything lifted over a fence; tilt-tray for 10ft and 20ft into town blocks and the industrial estates
locations.metaDesc: Shipping containers for sale and hire in Alice Springs. Delivered up or down the Stuart Highway for Central Australian stations, communities and trades.
locations.line: There is no short way into Alice Springs. It is about fifteen hundred kilometres down the Stuart from Darwin and roughly the same again up from Adelaide, so whichever direction a container comes from it is a multi-day linehaul before anybody so much as thinks about a crane. The upside is that the Stuart is sealed the whole way and the corridor is busy, so a container bound for the Alice is not an exotic request. It is a matter of getting it onto a truck already making the trip, and that is mostly a question of notice.
locations.uses: swag, trailer and camping gear storage for tour operators shutting down between seasons, staging and resupply storage for remote community stores and contractors working out of town, secure storage for art centres holding stock and materials, parts and workshop storage across the Ciccone, Arunga Park and Brewer Estate industrial areas, fodder, fencing and machinery storage on the pastoral country out along the Plenty, Tanami and Larapinta, site stores on remote build packages, and household storage for people posted into town before a house comes free
access: Alice Springs is a town shaped by a gap in a mountain range, and that geography shows up in delivery planning. Heavitree Gap is the only way in or out to the south for road and rail, and it is a genuine pinch point: two lanes, the river beside it, and when the Todd runs after heavy rain the road through it can close. It rarely lasts long, but it can strand a truck on the wrong side of town for a day. North of the gap the town is comfortable. Braitling, Larapinta, Gillen and the newer parts of Sadadeen have wide streets and driveways a rigid can get square to, and the industrial ground at Ciccone, Arunga Park and out at Brewer Estate is exactly what you would want: flat, hard, and used to trucks. The Old Eastside streets are tighter, with river gums over the road, narrow verges and services on the frontage, so a crane over the fence is often the sensible call there. Ground across the district is generally very good. Compacted red gravel and gibber carry a container without complaint and often need very little under them. Two exceptions: the sandy country along the Todd and the other creek lines, which is loose and deep, and any pad graded in the last few months and never compacted. The other planning factor is heat and light. Through summer the useful working window is the morning, because steel that has been in the sun since seven is unmanageable by lunchtime. In winter you get the reverse problem, with frost on the ground at dawn and a cold start. Send photos of the street, the run in and the spot itself, tell us whether the last leg is sealed, and we will tell you which truck is coming and roughly when.

sections.h: Fifteen hundred kilometres either way
p: The Alice sits almost exactly halfway between Darwin and Adelaide, which is either a curse or a convenience depending on how you look at it. It is a curse because there is no short run, no local depot around the corner, and no possibility of a same-week delivery for somebody who rings on a Friday having forgotten. It is a convenience because the Stuart Highway is one of the busiest freight corridors in the country and there is nearly always something moving in one direction or the other. A container that can wait for the right truck travels far more sensibly than one that cannot.

What that means in practice is notice. Two to four weeks is the usual window, and the customers who get the best of that range are the ones who ring early with a window rather than a deadline. Batching matters too: if a job needs two or three units, ordering them as a group gets them onto one run. And getting the specification right before the container leaves is worth real money out here, because sending a wrong unit back down the Stuart is not a small correction. Ring 1300 467 776 with the address, the job and what is going inside, and we will quote the container and the cartage as a single figure with nothing waiting on the invoice.

sections.h: A thirty degree swing between afternoon and dawn
p: Central Australia does something to a steel box that coastal towns do not. A forty degree February afternoon followed by a night that drops into the teens, or a twenty degree July day followed by a frost, means the container is expanding and contracting hard every twenty-four hours, and any moisture inside it condenses on the roof and walls overnight and drips back down. People call it container rain and it surprises anybody who assumed the desert was too dry for a moisture problem. It is not the humidity that does it, it is the temperature swing.

The fixes are cheap and they work. Ventilation first: standard vents help, whirlybirds help more, and cross-flow is better than a single opening. Then get the gear up off the floor on pallets so anything that does drip has somewhere to go. Do not store anything damp inside a sealed container and expect it to dry out on its own. And set it up off the ground on pads so air moves under the floor, which also keeps the underside out of the dust. If you are storing paper, textiles, artwork or anything with electronics in it, mention that when you order and we will spec the ventilation properly rather than leaving you to retrofit it.

sections.h: Deliveries beyond the Alice
p: A lot of Central Australian containers go a long way past the town. Stations and communities out along the Tanami, the Plenty, the Mereenie Loop and the Sandover, and the run south toward Yulara or north to Ti Tree and beyond. Two things decide whether those deliveries work. The first is the road. Unsealed sections corrugate, wash out and close entirely after rain, and a road that a station ute uses without thinking about it is not necessarily a road for a loaded truck. Local road reports and a bit of patience are part of the job. The second is what is at the far end, because a remote site with no loader means we have to bring the lifting capability with us and that changes the truck.

Access to Aboriginal land generally requires a permit, and that is arranged through the relevant land council or the community rather than by us. It is routine, but it takes lead time and it cannot be organised on the morning of a delivery, so raise it with us at the quote stage and we will work the timing around it. The same goes for community store hours, cultural obligations and the local contact who will actually be there when the truck arrives. Deliveries out here go smoothly when all of that is settled a fortnight in advance and badly when it is not.

faqs.q: How long does delivery to Alice Springs take?
faqs.a: Two to four weeks from order to on the ground is the normal window. The Stuart Highway is sealed the whole way from both Darwin and Adelaide and it is a busy corridor, so the timing is really about when a truck is running with room on the deck rather than about the distance itself. Units needing modification first, a personnel door, extra vents or paint, add a few days. If you have a fixed date, a lease start, a tour season, a site handover, tell us at the enquiry and give us as much notice as the job allows.

faqs.q: Can you deliver out to a station or a remote community from Alice Springs?
faqs.a: Yes, out along the Tanami, the Plenty, the Mereenie Loop, the Sandover and south toward Yulara. Three things we need. The state of the road, honestly, because unsealed sections corrugate and close after rain and a station road is not automatically a truck road. Whether there is a loader or telehandler at the far end, because if there is not we bring the lifting gear and that changes the truck. And permits, since access to Aboriginal land is arranged through the land council or community and takes lead time. Raise all three at the quote stage.

faqs.q: Do containers get condensation in the desert?
faqs.a: Yes, more than people expect, and the reason is the temperature swing rather than humidity. A hot afternoon followed by a cold night makes moisture inside condense on the roof and drip back onto whatever is below it. Ventilation is the answer: vents at minimum, whirlybirds if the contents matter, and openings at both ends so air actually crosses through. Store gear on pallets rather than flat on the floor, and never shut damp equipment inside and expect it to dry. Tell us what is going in and we will spec the ventilation before it leaves rather than after.

faqs.q: Can I inspect the container before it comes to Alice Springs?
faqs.a: Stock for Central Australia comes off our Darwin depot or off an eastern states run, and inspection at a depot is by arrangement rather than a walk-in, so ring 1300 467 776 first if you want to organise it. For most Alice Springs buyers that is not practical, so ask for photos of the actual unit on request and we will send them before delivery: the corner castings, both ends, the roof and a shot down the length of the floor. If anything in those photos is not what you were expecting, we deal with it before the container gets on a truck.
